The Great Reclamation: Why America Must Confiscate Extreme Private Wealth

A Persuasive Argument for a One-Time Wealth Ceiling of $10 Million

Introduction: The Arithmetic of Moral Emergency

There are approximately 22 million people in the United States who cannot afford adequate food. Roughly 582,000 sleep without shelter on any given night. Forty-five million carry student debt that structurally prevents them from building lives. Thirty million lack health insurance. Meanwhile, the combined wealth of American billionaires exceeded $4.5 trillion as of recent estimates — wealth accumulated not merely through individual genius or effort, but through decades of systematic policy choices, legal architecture, inherited advantage, and the labor of millions of people who received only a fraction of the value they generated.

This is not a paradox. It is a policy outcome. And policy outcomes can be changed by policy decisions.

The proposal advanced in this essay is straightforward, if politically unprecedented in modern America: a one-time, comprehensive state confiscation of all private wealth holdings above $10 million per individual or household, with the proceeds directed toward a constitutionally protected public trust funding healthcare, housing, education, and environmental restoration. This is not a tax. It is not a levy, a surcharge, or a disincentive. It is a democratic reclamation — a society deciding, collectively and democratically, that no private person requires more than ten million dollars to live an extraordinarily comfortable life, and that the remainder belongs to the civilization that made it possible.

The arguments for this policy are moral, economic, democratic, and practical. They are serious. They deserve serious engagement.

Part One: The Moral Case — Wealth Beyond Sufficiency Is a Form of Theft

The most fundamental argument for a wealth ceiling is philosophical, and it begins with a simple question: on what ethical basis does any individual claim ownership of $100 million, $1 billion, or $100 billion?

Defenders of extreme wealth typically invoke one of two justifications: desert (they earned it) or rights (property rights are sacrosanct). Both collapse under examination.

The desert argument fails empirically. The mythology of the self-made billionaire is precisely that — mythology. Jeff Bezos did not build the internet. Elon Musk did not invent battery chemistry, rocket physics, or the satellite communication infrastructure his companies exploit. Mark Zuckerberg did not develop the social psychology that makes human beings crave connection. Every fortune above a certain threshold is built on a foundation of public investment: government-funded research that produced the internet, GPS, touchscreens, and mRNA technology; public education that trained the engineers and workers; public roads and ports that move goods; legal systems that enforce contracts; and, critically, the labor of millions of workers whose wages were systematically suppressed below the value they produced.

The philosopher John Rawls argued that the natural talents and circumstances that allow people to succeed are "arbitrary from a moral point of view" — no one deserves to be born with exceptional intelligence, in a wealthy zip code, or at the precise historical moment when a particular skill becomes extraordinarily valuable. The worker who would have been a billionaire had she been born thirty years later and channeled into tech rather than manufacturing is morally indistinguishable from the actual billionaire. Their different outcomes reflect luck, not desert.

When we examine a $10 billion fortune, a more accurate accounting attributes perhaps a few million dollars to the individual's genuine contribution, and the remainder to the social infrastructure they inherited, the workers they employed at below-market-clearing wages, the monopoly rents they extracted through market dominance, and the tax avoidance strategies that shifted their obligations onto ordinary citizens. By this accounting, extreme wealth is not already-earned money being confiscated — it is already-owed money being collected.

The property rights argument is circular. Property rights are not natural phenomena discovered carved in granite. They are legal constructs created and maintained by the state — which means they exist at the society's pleasure and in service of social purposes. John Locke, the philosopher most associated with strong property rights, stipulated that private appropriation was legitimate only when "enough and as good" was left for others. By any honest accounting, a world in which 700 individuals control more wealth than the bottom half of humanity combined violates Locke's own proviso. The classical liberal tradition that conservatives claim as authority for extreme property rights already contains within it the justification for limiting those rights when they become incompatible with others' access to a decent life.

Furthermore, a $10 million threshold is extraordinarily generous. Ten million dollars, properly managed, generates passive income of $300,000–$500,000 annually without touching the principal. This is not poverty. This is not even constraint. This is generational security, total freedom from financial stress, and the ability to live at the highest levels of comfort available to human beings. The argument that confiscating wealth above this threshold constitutes oppression requires one to demonstrate what legitimate human purpose requires $100 million, $1 billion, or more — a demonstration that has never been successfully made.

Part Two: The Economic Case — Extreme Wealth Concentration Is Economically Destructive

Proponents of concentrated wealth often argue that billionaires "create value" and that restricting their accumulation would impoverish everyone. The economic evidence suggests the opposite: extreme wealth concentration is a drag on growth, a driver of instability, and a mechanism for entrenching privilege at the expense of broadly shared prosperity.

The velocity of money argument. A dollar held in a billionaire's portfolio moves through the economy very differently than a dollar in the hands of a working family. The working family spends it immediately on goods and services, creating demand that employs other workers, who then spend their wages, creating further demand — the economic multiplier. The billionaire's dollar, by contrast, is far more likely to be invested in financial instruments, real estate speculation, or offshore accounts, where it circulates within the financial system without generating equivalent real economic activity. The Federal Reserve's own research has documented how rising wealth concentration at the top has suppressed consumer demand and contributed to the secular stagnation that has characterized the American economy since the 1980s.

The misallocation of capital. Extreme private wealth concentrations direct capital based on the preferences of very few individuals rather than the democratic preferences of society. This is why we have seventeen flavors of social media platforms and insufficient housing; why we have a thriving private rocket industry and crumbling public transit systems; why we have luxury goods markets booming while clean water infrastructure in Flint goes unrepaired. The argument that billionaires "allocate capital efficiently" assumes their preferences align with social welfare — an assumption that requires ignoring everything we know about incentives, power, and the systematic divergence between private and social returns to investment.

The inheritance and dynasty problem. Extreme wealth accumulations do not stay with the "self-made" individual who allegedly earned them. They transfer to children who did nothing to earn them, creating a hereditary aristocracy that compounds across generations. Research by economists Raj Chetty and colleagues has documented how catastrophically low intergenerational mobility has become in the United States. A society in which your life outcomes are more strongly predicted by your parents' income than by your own initiative is not a market meritocracy — it is a feudal system with better branding.

The productive investment argument. The proceeds from a one-time wealth confiscation above $10 million would, by conservative estimates, generate somewhere in the range of $30–50 trillion (depending on methodology and valuation), with a more commonly cited figure for all wealth above $10M being in the range of $40+ trillion. Even directing a fraction of this toward public investment in education, healthcare, housing, and infrastructure would produce documented economic returns substantially exceeding the private returns that capital was generating in the hands of the wealthy. Universal pre-K has been shown to generate returns of $7–12 per dollar invested. Infrastructure investment has fiscal multipliers well above 1. Universal healthcare would eliminate the enormous deadweight loss of the administrative burden of America's private insurance system, which consumes 30 cents of every healthcare dollar in overhead that produces no medical care whatsoever.

Part Three: The Democratic Case — You Cannot Have Political Democracy With Economic Oligarchy

The argument that receives insufficient attention in discussions of wealth inequality is the democratic one, because it is perhaps the most powerful.

Democracy requires that citizens exercise approximately equal political power — that each person's voice counts roughly as much as any other's. This is the foundational principle. It is stated in the Declaration of Independence. It is the premise of one person, one vote. It is the justification for everything the American governmental system claims for itself.

Extreme wealth concentration makes this principle a fiction.

The mechanism is well-documented. The Princeton study by Gilens and Page, analyzing 1,779 policy outcomes over twenty years, found that the preferences of average Americans had "near-zero" impact on actual policy outcomes, while the preferences of economic elites and organized business interests had substantial and consistent influence. This is not conspiracy theory. This is peer-reviewed political science. Wealthy individuals and their affiliated corporations spend billions annually on campaign contributions, lobbying, funding think tanks that produce favorable "research," and capturing regulatory agencies staffed by former industry employees. The result is a political system that systematically produces policy favorable to the wealthy and systematically ignores the preferences of everyone else.

This is not democracy. It is a plutocracy with democratic aesthetics.

The solution requires eliminating the source of the distortion. Campaign finance reform, lobbying restrictions, and ethics rules are all valuable, but they address symptoms rather than causes. As long as there exist individuals with $10 billion, $50 billion, or $200 billion in private wealth, they possess the material capacity to distort democracy beyond the corrective capacity of regulatory tweaks. A person with $200 billion can spend $1 billion annually on political influence and barely notice the expenditure. No disclosure requirement eliminates this power asymmetry.

One-time wealth confiscation above $10 million eliminates the structural source of oligarchic power. It does not merely constrain it. It removes the material basis for political dominance by private economic actors. The result would not be a perfect democracy, but it would be a democracy with a fighting chance.

The historical precedent. Every functioning democracy that has maintained robust democratic institutions over time — the Scandinavian social democracies, postwar Western European democracies — has done so in part through aggressive redistribution that prevented the consolidation of oligarchic economic power. The United States had its most democratic period — the postwar decades of broadly shared prosperity, high union membership, and responsive government — during an era of high progressive taxation that functionally capped the concentration of political-economic power. The decline of those constraints has tracked precisely with the decline of democratic responsiveness documented by political scientists.

Part Four: The Practical Case — The Public Sector Is Catastrophically Underfunded

Abstract arguments about justice and democracy become concrete when you examine the actual state of American public institutions.

The American Society of Civil Engineers gives American infrastructure a grade of C-. The United States spends more per capita on healthcare than any other developed nation while producing worse health outcomes than all comparable countries. American students rank middling internationally in educational achievement. Public housing waitlists in major cities stretch to decades. Climate infrastructure necessary to prevent catastrophic warming requires trillions in investment that the private sector, responding to short-term profit incentives, will not provide.

These are not problems of insufficient national wealth. The United States is the wealthiest nation in the history of human civilization. The problem is that the wealth is sequestered in private holdings that produce no public benefit.

A one-time wealth confiscation above $10 million would generate public resources on a scale that could:

  • Eliminate all medical debt immediately (estimated at $140 billion)
  • Fund universal pre-K and childcare comprehensively for decades
  • Fully fund the Green New Deal's most ambitious climate provisions
  • Eliminate student debt entirely (approximately $1.7 trillion)
  • Repair and modernize all critical infrastructure
  • Establish a universal basic income program on a permanent, endowed basis
  • Create a sovereign wealth fund whose returns would permanently fund public programs without requiring ongoing taxation

This is not fantasy. These are arithmetic facts about what becomes possible when trillions of dollars shift from private investment portfolios into democratic public control.

Part Five: Responding to the Objections

"This is unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause."

The Takings Clause prohibits taking private property for public use without just compensation. However, the constitutional framework for property rights is not static, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld progressive taxation, including highly progressive estate taxation, as constitutional. More fundamentally, a democratic society has the power to amend its constitution, and if the existing constitutional framework cannot accommodate the democratic will of the people to limit extreme wealth concentration, that is an argument for constitutional amendment, not for accepting the permanence of oligarchy. It is worth noting that during World War II, the federal government exercised sweeping powers to commandeer private resources that would have been considered unthinkable in peacetime — the moral emergency of extreme poverty and failing public institutions is no less real than the emergency of wartime, merely less dramatic in its urgency.

"The wealthy will flee to other countries."

This objection assumes that people with $10 million and below — who would retain all of their wealth — would flee, which is implausible. Those above the threshold would have their wealth confiscated before any flight could occur, since the measure would necessarily be enacted with immediate effect. Furthermore, the empirical evidence on so-called "wealth flight" in response to taxation is considerably weaker than its proponents claim — studies of wealth taxes in European countries have found far less flight than predicted, particularly when the tax is comprehensive and the destination countries impose their own obligations. A world in which extreme wealth concentration is globally recognized as a democratic emergency would produce international coordination on this front, just as it has produced coordination on tax havens and financial transparency.

"Innovation will be destroyed without the incentive of unlimited wealth accumulation."

This argument requires us to believe that the prospect of accumulating $10 million — a fortune that provides complete material security for generations — is insufficient incentive to innovate. This is not credible. The most significant innovations in human history, including the internet, GPS, the World Wide Web, vaccines, and the Green Revolution, were produced by publicly funded researchers motivated by curiosity, public benefit, and professional recognition — not by the prospect of billions in personal wealth. The claim that innovation depends on the specific incentive of unlimited accumulation above $10 million has no serious empirical support. It is an ideological assertion masquerading as economic theory.

"This is communism."

A One-Time Wealth Reset for Economic Justice

The United States faces a profound crisis of inequality that no incremental policy has resolved. The richest 0.1 percent now hold more wealth than the bottom 90 percent combined, with private holdings exceeding $10 million frequently signaling concentrations that distort markets, politics, and opportunity. A bold, one-time large-scale confiscation of all private wealth above a high threshold—say, $10 million—offers the most direct, decisive intervention. By seizing excess accumulations and redirecting them into universal public programs, this measure would fund essential services from cradle to grave, dismantle structural barriers, and restore a measure of economic fairness without creating ongoing disincentives. Far from radical experimentation, it represents a rational corrective to a system where private concentration has crowded out public capacity.

The empirical case is stark. Median household wealth stagnates while the top decile has captured the majority of gains since the 1980s. Billionaire fortunes alone surpass the GDP of many nations, yet these holdings often function as idle capital, deployed in speculative markets rather than productive investment. A one-time levy above $10 million would target only the extreme tail—approximately the wealthiest 0.10–0.15 percent of households—drawing from data showing net worth in this cohort routinely reaches tens or hundreds of millions. Even with conservative estimates of $40–60 trillion in total U.S. wealth, the taxable portion above the cutoff could yield several trillion dollars when structured to include liquid assets, equities, and real property holdings net of legitimate liabilities.

These proceeds would transform public provision. Allocating half to a universal basic infrastructure fund could immediately retrofit infrastructure, expand high-speed rail, broadband, and clean energy grids, creating millions of high-wage jobs that private markets have failed to deliver at scale. Another quarter could seed a permanent endowment for universal pre-K, debt-free public higher education, and lifelong retraining accounts, erasing the lottery of birth that determines access today. Remaining resources could underwrite a national health service, eldercare expansion, and targeted reparations-style investments in communities historically excluded from asset accumulation. The result would be broad-based human capital development that raises productivity, reduces fiscal pressure on future budgets, and generates multiplier effects far exceeding the initial transfer.

Because it is explicitly one-time, current owners of wealth above the threshold retain clear title to the remaining $10 million plus any new accumulation thereafter. Post-confiscation tax rates can remain modest on ongoing income and new enterprise, preserving the reward for innovation and risk-taking that standard economic theory requires. Historical precedent supports feasibility: the United States financed World War II with effective wealth drawdowns through bond drives and progressive taxation far steeper in marginal impact than a single reset would impose. Wealth holders responded by reallocating into productive wartime production rather than permanent withdrawal. Modern capital is even more mobile and liquid than mid-century industrial assets; a time-limited, transparent seizure with judicial oversight can be administered before markets fully anticipate and evade it. Any flight occurs once, after which the remaining wealth distribution becomes self-sustaining.

Opponents further argue that inequality reflects merit and that confiscation punishes success. This view collapses under examination. Large-scale holdings today derive substantially from network effects, inherited advantages, regulatory capture, and asset inflation fueled by monetary policy that benefits owners rather than laborers. Survey data and mobility studies consistently show that parental wealth predicts adult outcomes more strongly than cognitive ability or educational attainment. The deeper justification lies in the social contract. When extreme private concentrations extract disproportionate shares of those goods while under-contributing to their upkeep, the bargain frays. Introduction

The Scale of Contemporary Wealth Concentration

Current wealth distribution patterns in many developed economies have reached levels not seen since the early 20th century. In the United States, the top 1% of households control approximately 32% of total wealth, while the bottom 50% hold just 2%. This concentration has accelerated dramatically over recent decades, with technological changes, globalization, and policy shifts creating unprecedented opportunities for wealth accumulation at the highest levels.

Proponents of wealth redistribution argue that such extreme concentration creates multiple systemic risks: it undermines democratic institutions through outsized political influence, reduces economic mobility, dampens consumer demand, and creates financial instability. Theoretical Framework for Wealth Redistribution

Advocates for large-scale wealth reallocation draw on several economic and philosophical traditions. From a utilitarian perspective, they argue that the marginal utility of wealth decreases dramatically at extremely high levels—an additional million dollars provides negligible benefit to someone with a $50 million portfolio but could transform public education in an entire school district.

Addressing Implementation Challenges

Critics consistently raise several implementation concerns that proponents attempt to address:

Asset Valuation and Liquidity: Supporters acknowledge that valuing complex assets like private businesses, art, or real estate presents challenges. They propose creating specialized federal assessment agencies, similar to those used for estate taxation, and allowing payment plans or asset transfers to address liquidity concerns.

Capital Flight: While acknowledging this risk, proponents argue that most ultra-wealthy individuals have deep ties to their home countries and cannot easily relocate all assets. They often propose coordination with international tax authorities and temporary capital controls during implementation.

Economic Disruption: Advocates contend that careful implementation could minimize market disruption while generating enormous public benefits. They argue that the wealth involved often represents financial assets rather than productive capital, limiting direct economic impact.

Supporters envision using revenue from wealth reallocation to address critical public needs:

  • Education Investment: Universal pre-K, student debt relief, and higher education access
  • Healthcare Access: Expanding public health programs and reducing medical debt
  • Climate Response: Accelerating clean energy transitions and climate adaptation
  • Social Safety Net: Strengthening unemployment insurance and poverty reduction programs

Precedents and Models

Advocates point to historical precedents for large-scale wealth redistribution, including:

  • Post-World War II wealth taxes in several European countries
  • Land redistribution programs in various nations
  • The successful implementation of estate taxation
  • Emergency economic measures during national crises

They argue that contemporary wealth concentration represents a comparable crisis requiring extraordinary response.

Democratic and Social Justice Arguments

Beyond economic considerations, supporters frame wealth redistribution as essential for democratic governance. They contend that extreme wealth concentration allows small groups to exercise disproportionate political influence through campaign contributions, lobbying, and media ownership. A one-time wealth levy could help restore more balanced democratic participation.

From a social justice perspective, advocates argue that extreme wealth often reflects systemic advantages—including inherited wealth, educational opportunities, and policy environments shaped by previous generations—rather than purely individual merit. They contend that society has legitimate claims on wealth that exceeds what any individual could reasonably accumulate through their own efforts.

Conclusion

While implementing a large-scale wealth levy would face significant practical and political challenges, proponents argue that the severity of contemporary inequality justifies considering dramatic policy interventions. They contend that traditional approaches have proven insufficient to address wealth concentration that threatens both economic stability and democratic governance.

The proposal represents one end of a spectrum of policy approaches to inequality, from incremental tax reforms to comprehensive wealth redistribution. The Case for a One-Time Levy on Extreme Wealth

Modern economies depend on public institutions: courts that enforce contracts, schools that educate workers, infrastructure that connects markets, scientific research that enables innovation, and financial systems stabilized by government action during crises. Yet in many countries, these foundations are strained while private wealth has become extraordinarily concentrated. A carefully designed, one-time levy on net wealth above a very high threshold—such as $10 million—would be a justified and practical way to strengthen essential public programs while asking the greatest contribution from those most capable of making it.

The central argument is one of shared obligation. Large fortunes do not arise in isolation. They are built within legal and economic systems maintained collectively: limited-liability corporations, intellectual-property protections, public infrastructure, central-bank stability, educated workforces, and reliable systems of property and contract law. Individual talent and risk-taking matter, but so do these public foundations. When those foundations require major reinvestment, people who have benefited most from them can reasonably be asked to contribute more.

A one-time levy would also address an imbalance that ordinary income taxes often miss. The wealthiest households frequently hold much of their economic power through appreciating assets rather than wages. Depending on the jurisdiction, gains may remain untaxed until assets are sold, receive favorable rates, or escape taxation through sophisticated estate and trust arrangements. Consequently, two households with radically different resources may face tax burdens that do not reflect their actual ability to pay. A levy on net wealth above a high exemption would reach accumulated economic capacity more directly.

The threshold is crucial. A $10 million exemption would protect ordinary savings, retirement accounts, homes, and most family businesses. The levy would apply only to the portion of net wealth above that amount, not to the first $10 million. Rates could be graduated, with a modest rate immediately above the threshold and higher rates for fortunes in the hundreds of millions or billions. Payment could be spread over several years so that owners of illiquid businesses, farms, or other hard-to-sell assets would not be forced into sudden liquidation.

The revenue should be dedicated to investments with broad and durable benefits. Potential uses include repairing water systems and transportation networks, expanding healthcare access, building affordable housing, reducing child poverty, improving public schools, funding climate resilience, and supporting scientific research. Such spending would not merely redistribute existing resources; it could increase productivity by producing a healthier, better-educated workforce and more reliable infrastructure. Investments in children, preventive medicine, and early education can also reduce future public costs.

The measure could promote economic justice without denying the legitimacy of success. Under a high exemption and graduated rates, wealthy households would retain substantial fortunes and continue to enjoy exceptional security and opportunity. The proposal would not seek equality of outcome. Introduction

This inequality is unsustainable. It is time to address the root causes and create a more just society.

The confiscation would not target the majority of wealth holders, which are ordinary families and small businesses. Instead, it would focus on the top 0.1% of the population, who hold more than 90% of global wealth. The confiscated wealth could fund a wide range of vital public programs, including:

Prompt:
Draft a passionate speech that strongly advocates for a one-time confiscation of excessive wealth above a fixed high threshold to redistribute resources fairly and to reduce extreme economic inequality.
Model Response:

Friends, neighbors, fellow human beings! Look around you. Look at the world we live in. Side-by-side exist unimaginable luxury and soul-crushing poverty. While a tiny fraction of our population hoards wealth beyond comprehension – yachts, private islands, fortunes that dwarf nations – millions struggle to afford their next meal, a roof over their heads, healthcare for their children. This is not merely an economic imbalance; it is a moral failing, a wound on the soul of humanity, screaming out for justice.

The argument for pouring more fuel on this fire of inequality, for allowing the accumulation of wealth to grow unchecked, rings increasingly hollow. We hear of "trickle-down" effects, but all we see is wealth trickling upward. We hear about incentives for creation, but how much creation is driven by vanity and hoarding versus genuine societal need? We have reached a point of obscene excess where the question is no longer if we should act, but how quickly and decisively we can act to right this fundamental wrong.

Today, I call for a radical, yet incredibly necessary, step: A one-time, definitive confiscation and redistribution of wealth accumulated beyond a deliberately high, yet fair, threshold.

Let me be clear. This is not about punishing success. It is not about envy, nor is it communism. It is about recognizing that our current system, corrupted as it is by limitless concentration of capital, inherently generates injustice. It is about saying that there is a line beyond which the accumulation of wealth serves no positive purpose for society and actively harms the majority by starving them of resources.

Imagine, for a moment, we set that threshold at an amount that still allows immense personal comfort and legacy beyond the dreams of most. Let's say, for argument's sake, over a billion dollars for a single individual or entity. Any wealth above this threshold is currently doing absolutely nothing productive for our collective well-being. It contributes exactly zero to solving climate change, poverty, disease, or inequality. Instead, it often fuels speculation, instability, and further entrenchment of power.

Why one-time? Because we should not codify confiscation. This is about correcting centuries of distortion, the legacy of colonialism, exploitation, and unfair structures. It's a blow struck against the inertia of entrenched privilege, a moment to reset the balance before the chasm becomes unbridgeable. Future wealth creation is off the table for confiscation in this model. It targets only the already accumulated inequality that sits like a malevolent cancer in our global community.

Think of the possibilities if that hoarded wealth were brought back into the circulation of human need! Imagine:

  • The unemployed supported, not through endless welfare debates, but through dignified, temporary aid.
  • Our children educated in well-funded schools, with resources they desperately need, regardless of their parents' wealth.
  • Our vital healthcare systems, accessible to all, not just the privileged.
  • The transition to renewable energy accelerated, funded not by public taxes forever, but by a one-time realignment of massive resources.
  • The end of chronic homelessness, treated as the health and societal emergency it is.
  • A massive fund created to address the displacement, suffering, and conflict driven by desperate poverty.

Is this punitive? Hardly. It is redistributive – the ultimate fulfillment of the social contract. It is restorative – giving back some measure of equity to a system that has deliberately, for so long, denied it to the many for the benefit of the few. The beneficiaries of this confiscation and redistribution are not some faceless entity, but you, me, our children, our communities, our fragile planet.

The voices of those who profit from the imbalance will cry foul. They will invoke threats of capital flight or economic stagnation – hollow arguments protecting themselves from the gravity of the injustice they perpetrate. They will try to scare you. But we must be courageous. We must be humane. We must recognize that the fate of our shared humanity is not tied to the perpetuation of extreme, unnecessary wealth in the hands of the few, but in ensuring dignity and opportunity for all.

This is not a call for revolution in the sense of chaos. It is a call for radical fairness, for a fundamental recalibration of our economic DNA. It requires political will, courage, and a populace ready to demand justice.

Righting the wrongs of massive, unnecessary wealth requires action that is equally massive and determined. Let us resolve today, to stand together, to demand this justice, to reclaim our world's resources. Let us say loud and clear: Enough! We can do this, we must do this, to build a future where wealth serves humanity, not the other way around. Let this be the legacy we strive for.
